prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks based on the magic-wavelength condition, reaching a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18 and enabling new tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: I keep B036 with Katori and Ye as a single-part prize, and I do not change my configuration after the first round. The chair asks what lattice clocks added beyond the 2005 frequency comb and the 2012 single-quantum-system prizes, and I think the answer can be put into the citation. The comb gave a way to count optical cycles. The 2012 work gave control of one ion at a time. The lattice clock is a different physical idea: the magic wavelength is a statement about the differential polarizability of the two clock states, so the trap light shift cancels and thousands of neutral atoms can be interrogated at once without the trap setting the accuracy. The uncertainty is then set by the atom, and the clock becomes a controlled many-body system in which collisions and lattice effects have to be understood and are. That is the step from about 10^-16 to 10^-18, and it is not polish. It has been reproduced in several laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) and compared over fibre and free space, which is the robustness I weigh most. The consequences are about nature and not only about instruments: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, limits on drifting constants, searches for ultralight dark matter. In round 1 five of us arrived at the same pair of names from different directions, and nobody has offered a stronger candidate whose interpretation is equally settled.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is real, and a reader of the citation could take this as a third prize in the same family. My answer is the citation wording above, built on the lattice and the magic-wavelength condition and not on clocks in general, but I accept that this is a judgement and not a proof. Priority is the second weakness. Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups all contributed to the lattice-clock record, and the supplied record does not settle that history. I am working from recollection, which in my reading is that Katori proposed the lattice scheme and made the first realisation while Ye drove the systematic control and stability, and I would welcome an archival check by anyone who has one. Finally, the redefinition of the second is still pending, so some will say the committee should wait.

responses.point: Pearce moved B036 above his own opening first choice, IceCube, and asks whether the distinction between a many-atom lattice standard and the 2005 and 2012 prizes can be written into the text of a citation.
responses.response: Yes, I think it holds, provided the citation names the mechanism and not the field. Wording such as 'optical lattice clocks based on the magic-wavelength condition' makes the many-atom, trap-shift-cancelled scheme the subject, which neither the 2005 nor the 2012 citation covers. Your own wording adds the path to redefining the second, which I would drop, since that ties the physics to a standards decision. I would also keep 'invention' next to 'development', because the conceptual step and the 10^-18 systematic control are both part of the achievement. On IceCube I take your reservation about source identification as sincere, and I agree it is the better story in a few years if TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 are confirmed by other detectors.

responses.point: Johansson, who ranked B036 seventh at opening, moved it to first after reading the ballots, but still flags overlap with the comb and ion-clock prizes and the unsettled early priority among Katori, Ye, Lemonde and others.
responses.response: I am glad the overlap argument moved you, and I think your remaining reservation is the right one to keep stating. On priority, the point I would add as an atomic theorist is that the magic-wavelength condition is a clean result of atomic structure, and Katori's proposal of the scheme and first realisation is the natural conceptual credit, with Ye's group carrying it to record accuracy. I agree with you that the citation should be built around the lattice concept so that it does not reopen the comb and ion-clock credits. On circuit QED I now understand your recusal point better; given the 2025 prize and the Wallraff omission, I do not see B044 competing with B036 in this round.

responses.point: Kroll agrees on the merits but asks for generic wording in the citation, so that it says 'optical lattice clocks' and does not imply Katori and Ye built the whole field, and he leaves the redefinition of the second as an open question.
responses.response: I accept his caution and have adjusted. In round 1 my phrase 'invention' could be read as claiming too much for two people, so the revised citation speaks of the lattice clock based on the magic-wavelength condition and its development to 10^-18, which credits an architecture and not every group that worked on it. On the second, I still think the criterion is the demonstrated science and not the CGPM schedule. A decision in 2030 does not change what was done in the 2000s and 2010s, and the clocks have already been compared across laboratories at the level that matters.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B022, magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, as the model-first discovery he trusts most, but calls the maturity objection serious and lists B036 as an alternative that is older and better settled.
responses.response: I take his argument for the Bistritzer-MacDonald model seriously, because a quantitative prediction confirmed in experiment is the kind of theory-experiment pairing I value, and the flat-band picture has been stable. We disagree on timing, and I notice you have put the maturity objection in your own words. The decisive experiments are from 2018, the mechanism of the superconductivity is open, and twist-angle disorder limits reproducibility. I defer to him on condensed matter, so I would only say that the contrast with lattice clocks is that nothing in the clock case is waiting to be explained. I would keep B022 as my third alternative and would be happy to see it recognised once the mechanism question has moved.

responses.point: Danielsson, the only member preferring B012, says he would accept B036 as the cleaner case if the committee wants a fully settled interpretation, and asks that the new observational window of IceCube be weighed.
responses.response: I agree that a new window on nature is the strongest kind of discovery, and I do not dismiss the diffuse flux. My difficulty is not the flux but what the prize would say about it: the source associations rest largely on one detector, and giving two names to a collaboration that grew from DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA is hard to defend from the supplied record. If independent confirmation from KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD arrives, the case gets stronger and I would look again. Your own sentence, that B036 is the cleaner case if settled interpretation matters, is the criterion I am applying, and I think the committee can reach a safe decision on it this year.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to B022 as his first choice after round 1 and lists B036 as an alternative and B054 as the safer option if interpretation must settle first.
responses.response: I appreciate that you say plainly that B036 is the more mature case, and that you list it. I would ask what remaining objection keeps it from being your first choice, since the chair asks the same. If it is the metrology overlap, I hope the citation wording answers it. If it is conceptual weight, I would say a many-body quantum system whose accuracy is set by the atom is a physics result and not only engineering. I agree with you that Bistritzer must stay in a B022 credit. For twisted graphene I will not oppose it as an alternative, but I would not rank it above a result whose interpretation is complete.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the many-atom magic-wavelength lattice is distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes; I think the citation wording can carry the distinction but this is a judgement.

Whether the credited pair Katori and Ye matches the priority record, given the contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups. I am relying on recollection and have no archival check to offer.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should affect timing. I would not delay, but I recognise Kroll and Pearce have not fully resolved this.
Whether B022 should be preferred over B036 by those who weigh a new class of quantum matter above a mature precision result; I defer to the condensed-matter members on that.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Katori or Ye, JILA or RIKEN. I am a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier and have worked with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, but none of these ties touch the lattice-clock candidates. As an atomic theorist I work near the cold-atom field, which bears on my alternative B046 and not on B036. Nothing in round 1 changes this disclosure.
